## Introduction

Flooding is caused by many mechanisms, including when heavy rainfall causes rivers to overflow, when impervious surfaces reduce water infiltration, and/or when soil becomes oversaturated (@Javadinejad2022; @Lecce2000FloodTiming). Flash floods are considered to be one of the most severe natural disasters due to their rapid onset, unpredictability, infrastructure damage, and associated fatalities (@Diakakis2020; @Sadkou2024FlashFloods). Infrastructure and agricultural damage costs have steadily increased in the twentieth century (@Saharia2017). According to the IPCC, the severity and frequency of flood-causing severe storms will likely increase due to climate change (@IPCC2021Chapter11; @Halsnaes2023FloodModels). Due to Northwest Florida’s location relative to the Gulf of Mexico and major hurricane paths, most flooding research has focused on sea-level rise and coastal flooding, leaving inland flood risk understudied (@Bilskie2014Dynamics; @Morss2024Storm). Floods are extremely important to keep track of as they prove to contribute to human deaths, property damage, ecosystem changes, and social-economic losses (@Chen2020FloodSusceptibility). Growing evidence of machine learning models' capabilities to accurately predict storm severity and susceptibility highlights a major opportunity to apply these models to Northwest Florida (@Gensini2021SevereML; @Akshay2021FloodSeverity; @Chen2022RandomForestGeo).

Random Forest (RF) is a type of machine learning algorithm that predicts the dependent variable based on independent variables (@Salman2024RandomForest). RF is a smart model that uses simple models, aka decision trees (@Salman2024RandomForest). Errors produced by the random forest training can be counteracted by increasing the number of samples and trees of classification (@Wang2015FloodRF). Additionally, each decision tree’s selection of data is random, which prevents the model from memorizing the data (@Salman2024RandomForest). The RF application allowed for the importance of each variable to be assessed, and each index contribution to the overall risk was calculated pertaining to the relevant study of interest in China (@Wang2015FloodRF). The RF technique is optimal for performing hydrological studies due to the ability of the machine learning model to map flood risk analysis for hazard assessment with a low-cost application of the non-traditional model compared to rainfall-runoff models (@Zhu2022FloodRF). For instance,  a machine learning study in 2024 using 16 flood risk factors (FRFs), including historic flood damage locations, found that several high and very high flood risk areas closely overlapped with FEMA’s 100-year floodplain in Tampa Bay (@Dey2024). In another hydrological study, RF was able to reproduce the characteristics of the studied flood events and represented the daily flood discharge well in comparison with the hydromad modeling (@Schoppa2020RFDischarge). As research progresses, it is noted that identifying key driving factors and validating them via machine learning is a key driver in precision flood prediction (@Tan2024FlashFloodDrivers).

Northwest Florida, often referred to as the Florida Panhandle, is home to 16 counties: Escambia, Santa Rosa, Okaloosa, Walton, Holmes, Washington, Bay, Jackson, Calhoun, Gulf, Liberty, Franklin, Gadsden, Leon, Wakulla, and Jefferson. Since January 1996, these counties have had 1,052 floods, 790 of which were flash floods and 262 non-flash floods. Flooding has resulted in approximately $656 million in property damage throughout the counties, with Escambia County ranking number one in damage with approximately $152 million since 1996 (@NOAAStormEvents). This study will be utilizing RF to predict flood damage in Northwest Florida based on housing units, population, median home value, flood type (flash flood vs. flood), precipitation (1-day, 3-day, and 7-day cumulative amounts), and county. This type of RF modeling has not been used at a county level in Northwest Florida and most flooding research is focused on coastal flooding due to the counties being in major hurricane paths. This is important because floods are not uniform for every county and mitigation planning is an important part of preparing for natural hazards. 

## Methods

Random Forest is a supervised machine learning algorithm that introduces two sources of randomness during training. First, it uses bootstrap sampling of the training data, meaning data points are randomly selected with replacement so that the same data point may appear multiple times in a tree’s training sample, while others may not appear at all. Second, at each split within a tree, a random subset of predictor variables is considered when determining the best split. A tree continues to split until further splitting stops improving prediction or a preset depth limit is reached (@Dutta2023COVIDML).

In Random Forest a tree will start at a root node containing all sampled data points. Then it chooses a variable to split the data (i.e. flood versus flash flood) then splits all sampled data points by that criteria. (@Rigatti2017RandomForest) The tree creates splits on either side of the original split and then reorganizes the data points based on that criteria, as seen in @fig-random-forest. Each decision tree corresponds to the binary split of an explanatory variable: rainfall amount, flood type, or housing unit amount. Each decision produces an outcome determined by the algorithm to create a final prediction of flood damages using random forest for the Northwest Florida counties. 

```{dot}
//| label: fig-random-forest
//| fig-cap: "Conceptual representation of the random forest algorithm"
//| fig-width: 8
//| out-width: 100%
//| fig-align: center
digraph random_forest_example {
  graph [layout = dot, rankdir = TB, compound = true]
  node [shape = box, style = filled, fillcolor = chartreuse3, fontname = Helvetica]
  
  final [shape = ellipse, label = "Final Prediction\n(Average of Trees)"]

  subgraph cluster_1 {
    label = "Tree 1"
    t1a [label = "Rainfall > 3 in?"]
    t1d [label = "High Damage"]
    t1e [label = "Low Damage"]
    t1a -> t1d [label = "Yes"]
    t1a -> t1e [label = "No"]
  }
  
  subgraph cluster_2 {
    label = "Tree 2"
    t2a [label = "Flood Type = Flash Flood?"]
    t2d [label = "High Damage"]
    t2e [label = "Moderate Damage"]
    t2a -> t2d [label = "Yes"]
    t2a -> t2e [label = "No"]
  }

  subgraph cluster_3 {
    label = "Tree 3"
    t3a [label = "Housing Units > 50,000?"]
    t3d [label = "Moderate Damage"]
    t3e [label = "Low Damage"]
    t3a -> t3d [label = "Yes"]
    t3a -> t3e [label = "No"]
  }

  t1d -> final
  t1e -> final
  t2d -> final
  t2e -> final
  t3d -> final
  t3e -> final
}
```
Random forest is a flexible, buildable, and straightforward machine learning method. Random forest produces hundreds of decision trees and binary splitting to determine the best split per possible variable. Each tree is trained with a random parameter, and the splitting function is used for the selection of the more fitting observable variable. Random forest can handle different feature types of binary, categorical, and numeric data for the use of classification, clustering, and/or regression analysis. The random forest method ensembles powerful extractions and applications of information with decision trees utilized in its model structure (@Speiser2019RandomForest).

Random forest regression analysis is capable of handling large datasets and computing the variable importance of each data component. Random forest is capable of handling highly dimensional data as it produces regression trees with binary splits for outcome predictions. Random forest applies to the flood damage prediction method as it determines the model’s accuracy for optimal predictors of the dataset based on variable selection and statistical characteristics. The three datasets chosen for our prediction analysis require decision-making to develop the outcome of interest of flood damage prediction (@Haddouchi2019RandomForest).

### Formula

Mean square error is used in random forest regression to determine the optimal splits during training and evaluate the model performance. The lower mean square error that is determined, the greater the model accuracy. The squared difference between actual and predicted values is squared (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)². 1 over the number of observations averages the total squared error. The summation symbol Σ represents the summation of the observed data points (@hodson2021mean).

$$
MSE = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2
$$

### Assumptions

* Each tree makes its own decisions.
* Data points are chosen randomly to reduce mistakes.
* Sufficient data ensures the trees have unique patterns and variety.
* Combining the predictions from different trees leads to a more accurate final result.

### Advantages

* Easy to identify importance of features
* Multiple decision trees tend to cause little risk of overfitting (not too close to original training data)
* Very accurate due to multiple subgroups
* Less need for data management (pre-processing to perform random forest)

### Limitations

* Slower to acquire observations for best decision making
* Bound by the lowest and highest observations (no extrapolate)
* Difficult to interpret the decisions of ‘best features’ seen with trees## Data and Visualization

## Analysis and Results

### Data Discussion: 

Data collected for this project utilizes the [NOAA Storm Events Database](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/stormevents/); daily precipitation observations from the [Global Historical Climatology Network Daily (GHCN-Daily)](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/land-based-station/global-historical-climatology-network-daily); total population, total housing units, and median home value from the [American Community Survey 5-year estimates](https://data.census.gov/). Variables utilized in this study are listed in @tbl-table-one, including the source for each variable.

According to the data collected from NOAA, Northwest Florida expereienced 1,203 flooding events between January 1, 2000 and December 31, 2025. Flooding event distribution is represented in @fig-flood-event-pie. Of the flooding events, 77.1% are categorized as flash floods and 22.9% are categorized as floods. This data indicates that Northwest Florida counties experience short-duration, high-intensity rainfall events more often then long-duration rainfall events.

```{r}
#| label: fig-flood-event-pie
#| fig-cap: "Flash Flood vs Flood Events (2000–Present)"
#| fig-align: center

library(dplyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)

stormevents <- read_csv("StormEvents_NWFL2.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(BEGIN_DATE_TIME = mdy(BEGIN_DATE)) %>%
  filter(BEGIN_DATE_TIME >= as.Date("2000-01-01"))

floodcountall <- stormevents %>%
  count(EVENT_TYPE) %>%
  mutate(percent = n / sum(n) * 100)

ggplot(floodcountall, aes(x = "", y = percent, fill = EVENT_TYPE)) +
  geom_col(width = 1, color = "white") +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(percent, 1), "%\n(", n, ")")),
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
    color = "white",
    size = 6
  ) +
  labs(
    fill = "Event Type"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Flash Flood" = "blue2", "Flood" = "chartreuse3")) +
  theme_void()
```
Further breaking down the dataset, @fig-flood-events-county illustrates the number of flash flood and flood events by county. Bay County experiences the highest number of flooding events, with over 150 flash floods and approximately 30 flood events recorded between January 1, 2000 and December 31, 2025. In contrast, Liberty County experienced the fewest flood events, with fewer than 25 flash floods and fewer than 10 flood events during the same time period. This pattern is likely influence by the each county's geographic profile. Bay County has 708 square miles of water while Liberty County has only 7.6 square miles of water (@ACS2024).  

```{r}
#| label: fig-flood-events-county
#| fig-cap: "Flood and Flash Flood Events by County"
#| fig-align: center

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(suncalc)
library(lubridate)

stormevents <- stormevents %>%
  mutate(
    CZ_NAME_STR = case_when(
      CZ_NAME_STR == "JACKSON CO." ~ "Jackson County",
      CZ_NAME_STR == "OKALOOSA CO." ~ "Okaloosa County",
      CZ_NAME_STR == "JACKSON (ZONE)" ~ "Jackson County",
      TRUE ~ CZ_NAME_STR
    )
  )

stormevents %>%
  count(CZ_NAME_STR, EVENT_TYPE) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = CZ_NAME_STR, y = n, fill = EVENT_TYPE)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Flood" = "blue2", "Flash Flood" = "chartreuse3")) +
  labs(
    x = "County",
    y = "Number of Events",
    fill = "Event Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```

As discussed in the introduction, rainfall events are forecasted to increase in frequency and intensity. The NOAA data set from NOAA supports this pattern. In @fig-flood-damage-time yearly flood event totals and total damage are plotted for yearly from January 1, 2020 to December 31, 2025. On the right y-axis, property damage in millions is represented, and on the left y-axis, the number of flood events is represented The orange trend line tells us that the number of flood events is increasing (higher frequency). The red trend line shows us that the total property damage is slightly elevated across the 25 year period. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-flood-damage-time
#| fig-cap: "Flood Events and Property Damage Over Time"
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 7

library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)
library(ggplot2)

yearly_data <- stormevents %>%
  mutate(
    BEGIN_DATE = mdy(BEGIN_DATE),
    year = year(BEGIN_DATE),
    damage = as.numeric(DAMAGE_PROPERTY_NUM)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(year)) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    storms = n(),
    total_damage_millions = sum(damage, na.rm = TRUE) / 1000000,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

scale_factor <- max(yearly_data$storms, na.rm = TRUE) / 
  max(yearly_data$total_damage_millions, na.rm = TRUE)

ggplot(yearly_data, aes(x = year)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = storms, fill = "Flood Events"), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = total_damage_millions * scale_factor, color = "Total Damage"),
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(y = total_damage_millions * scale_factor, color = "Damage Trendline"),
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(y = storms, color = "Frequency Trendline"),
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Legend",
    values = c("Flood Events" = "blue3")
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    name = "Legend",
    values = c(
      "Total Damage" = "chartreuse3",
      "Damage Trendline" = "red",
      "Frequency Trendline" = "orange"
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Number of Flood Events",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(
      ~ . / scale_factor,
      name = "Total Property Damage (Millions of $)"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(min(yearly_data$year), max(yearly_data$year), by = 5)
  ) +
  labs(x = "Year") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

The table includes the population size, number of housing units, and the median home values for each of the 16 Northwest Florida counties from the 2024 survey.

Accurate representation of property damage is the essential to creating an accurate and usable model. Due to inflation, property damage values from 20 years ago is not an accurate representation of present day dollars. To improve accuraces,the NOAA data utilized for the model was reduced to the past six years, starting in January 2020. The sample size in this data range was large enough for the Random Forest Model, while portraying meaningful property damage amounts. 

To strengthen the model, rainfall data was collected from the [Global Historical Climatology Network Daily (GHCN-Daily)](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/land-based-station/global-historical-climatology-network-daily). Every county with the expection of Calhoun County, had precipitation gauges. For Calhoun County, precipitation data was collected from the four souronding counties (Bay,  Gulf, Jackson, and Libery Counties) and averaged per day. @fig-monthly-rainfall-county illustrates the monthly average rainfall per county in Northwest Florida.

```{r}
#| label: fig-monthly-rainfall-county
#| fig-cap: "Average Monthly Rainfall by County"
#| fig-align: center

library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)

prec <- read_xlsx("Precp.xlsx")

monthly_avg <- prec %>%
  mutate(
    DATE = as.Date(DATE),
    rain_in = PRCP,
    year = year(DATE),
    month_num = month(DATE),
    month = month(DATE, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(DATE), !is.na(rain_in)) %>%
  filter(year >= 2020, year <= 2025) %>%
  group_by(County, DATE, year, month_num, month) %>%
  summarise(daily_rain = mean(rain_in, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(County, year, month_num, month) %>%
  summarise(month_total = sum(daily_rain, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(County, month_num, month) %>%
  summarise(avg_monthly_rain_in = mean(month_total, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(County, month_num)

ggplot(monthly_avg, aes(x = month, y = avg_monthly_rain_in)) +
  geom_col(fill = "blue3") +
  facet_wrap(~ County, ncol = 4) +
  labs(
    x = "Month",
    y = "Average Rainfall (inches)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```
As shown in @fig-monthly-rainfall-county, rainfall amounts are highest during the summer months. However, @fig-monthly-flood-events indicates that flood events occur more frequently in September and April.

```{r}
#| label: fig-monthly-flood-events
#| fig-cap: "Average Number of Flood Events per Month"
#| fig-align: center

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)

monthly_floods <- stormevents %>%
  mutate(
    year = year(BEGIN_DATE_TIME),
    month = month(BEGIN_DATE_TIME, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)
  ) %>%
  group_by(year, month) %>%
  summarise(events = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(avg_events = mean(events))

ggplot(monthly_floods, aes(x = month, y = avg_events)) +
  geom_col(fill = "blue3") +
  labs(
    x = "Month",
    y = "Average Flood Events per Year"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()+
   theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```
In order to verify this theory, rainfall daily maximums were calcualted per month (@fig-max-daily-rainfall). This figures shows that rainfall daily maximums are highest in September, suggesting that September experiences high-intesntiy but less frequent rainfall events which may contribute to more frequent flooding events. 
```{r}
#| label: fig-max-daily-rainfall
#| fig-cap: "Maximum Daily Rainfall by Month"
#| fig-align: center

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)
library(ggplot2)

rain_intensity <- prec %>%
  filter(!is.na(DATE), !is.na(PRCP)) %>%
  mutate(
    month = month(DATE, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)
  ) %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(
    max_rain = max(PRCP),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(rain_intensity, aes(x = month, y = max_rain)) +
  geom_col(fill = "blue3") +
  labs(
    x = "Month",
    y = "Maximum Daily Rainfall (inches)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()+
   theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

### Random Forest 

<!--
The rainfall data had multiple gauges in each county, so I had to combine them.

At first, I thought about averaging, but that didn’t really make sense for flooding. Flooding is usually caused by the heaviest rainfall in an area, not the average.

So instead, I used the maximum rainfall per county per day.

Then I built:

1-day rainfall before the event
3-day total rainfall before the event
7-day total rainfall before the event

I also made sure:

every day existed (even if it was 0 rain)
missing values were treated as 0

The rainfall data had multiple gauges in each county, so I had to combine them.

At first, I thought about averaging, but that didn’t really make sense for flooding. Flooding is usually caused by the heaviest rainfall in an area, not the average.

So instead, I used the maximum rainfall per county per day.

Then I built:

1-day rainfall before the event
3-day total rainfall before the event
7-day total rainfall before the event

I also made sure:

every day existed (even if it was 0 rain)
missing values were treated as 0
-->

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(randomForest)
library(caret)
library(readxl)
library(zoo)

#-------------------------------
# 1. Flood events
#-------------------------------
flood_events <- stormevents %>%
  mutate(
    County = str_trim(CZ_NAME_STR),
    county_key = County %>%
      str_to_lower() %>%
      str_remove("\\s+county$") %>%
      str_trim(),
    BEGIN_DATE = mdy(BEGIN_DATE),
    EVENT_TYPE = str_trim(EVENT_TYPE)
  ) %>%
  filter(EVENT_TYPE %in% c("Flood", "Flash Flood")) %>%
  filter(BEGIN_DATE >= as.Date("2020-01-01")) %>%
  select(
    EVENT_ID,
    County,
    county_key,
    BEGIN_DATE,
    EVENT_TYPE,
    DAMAGE_PROPERTY_NUM,
    DAMAGE_CROPS_NUM,
    DEATHS_DIRECT,
    DEATHS_INDIRECT,
    INJURIES_DIRECT,
    INJURIES_INDIRECT,
    everything()
  )

nrow(flood_events)
table(flood_events$EVENT_TYPE)
names(flood_events)
```
```{r}
#-------------------------------
# 2. County daily rainfall
#    Use MAX across gauges, not MEAN
#-------------------------------
county_daily_rain <- prec %>%
  mutate(
    County = str_trim(County),
    county_key = County %>%
      str_to_lower() %>%
      str_remove("\\s+county$") %>%
      str_trim(),
    DATE = as.Date(DATE)
  ) %>%
  group_by(County, county_key, DATE) %>%
  summarise(
    PRCP = max(PRCP, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# this should return 0 rows
county_daily_rain %>%
  count(county_key, DATE) %>%
  filter(n > 1)
```
```{r}
#-------------------------------
# 3. Fill missing dates with 0 rain
#    so rolling windows are true 1-, 3-, and 7-day periods
#-------------------------------
county_daily_rain_complete <- county_daily_rain %>%
  group_by(County, county_key) %>%
  complete(
    DATE = seq(min(DATE, na.rm = TRUE), max(DATE, na.rm = TRUE), by = "day"),
    fill = list(PRCP = 0)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```
```{r}
#-------------------------------
# 4. Prior-day rainfall windows
#-------------------------------
county_rain_windows <- county_daily_rain_complete %>%
  arrange(county_key, DATE) %>%
  group_by(county_key) %>%
  mutate(
    rain_1day_prior = lag(PRCP, 1),
    rain_3day_prior = lag(
      rollapply(PRCP, width = 3, FUN = sum, align = "right", fill = NA, partial = FALSE),
      1
    ),
    rain_7day_prior = lag(
      rollapply(PRCP, width = 7, FUN = sum, align = "right", fill = NA, partial = FALSE),
      1
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    rain_1day_prior = replace_na(rain_1day_prior, 0),
    rain_3day_prior = replace_na(rain_3day_prior, 0),
    rain_7day_prior = replace_na(rain_7day_prior, 0)
  )
county_rain_windows %>%
  select(County, county_key, DATE, PRCP, rain_1day_prior, rain_3day_prior, rain_7day_prior) %>%
  mutate(
    across(c(PRCP, rain_1day_prior, rain_3day_prior, rain_7day_prior), ~ round(.x, 3))
  ) %>%
  print(n = 20)



```
```{r}
county_rain_windows <- county_daily_rain_complete %>%
  arrange(county_key, DATE) %>%
  group_by(county_key) %>%
  mutate(
    rain_1day_prior = lag(PRCP, 1),
    rain_3day_prior = lag(
      rollapply(PRCP, width = 3, FUN = sum, align = "right", fill = NA, partial = FALSE),
      1
    ),
    rain_7day_prior = lag(
      rollapply(PRCP, width = 7, FUN = sum, align = "right", fill = NA, partial = FALSE),
      1
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    rain_1day_prior = replace_na(rain_1day_prior, 0),
    rain_3day_prior = replace_na(rain_3day_prior, 0),
    rain_7day_prior = replace_na(rain_7day_prior, 0)
  )
```


```{r}
flood_with_rain <- flood_events %>%
  left_join(
    county_rain_windows %>%
      select(county_key, DATE, rain_1day_prior, rain_3day_prior, rain_7day_prior),
    by = c("county_key", "BEGIN_DATE" = "DATE")
  )
flood_with_context <- flood_with_rain %>%
  left_join(
    census_data %>%
      mutate(
        County = str_trim(County),
        county_key = County %>%
          str_to_lower() %>%
          str_remove("\\s+county$") %>%
          str_trim()
      ) %>%
      select(county_key, Population, HousingUnits, MedianHomeValue),
    by = "county_key"
  )

names(flood_with_context)

flood_with_context %>%
  select(County, Population, HousingUnits, MedianHomeValue) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  print(n = 20)
```
```{r}
flood_model_data <- flood_with_context %>%
  select(
    EVENT_ID,
    County,
    BEGIN_DATE,
    DAMAGE_PROPERTY_NUM,
    rain_1day_prior,
    rain_3day_prior,
    rain_7day_prior,
    Population,
    HousingUnits,
    MedianHomeValue
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    log_damage = log1p(DAMAGE_PROPERTY_NUM)
  )
```


```{r}
flood_model_data %>%
  summarise(
    damage_missing = sum(is.na(DAMAGE_PROPERTY_NUM)),
    rain1_missing = sum(is.na(rain_1day_prior)),
    rain3_missing = sum(is.na(rain_3day_prior)),
    rain7_missing = sum(is.na(rain_7day_prior)),
    pop_missing = sum(is.na(Population)),
    housing_missing = sum(is.na(HousingUnits)),
    value_missing = sum(is.na(MedianHomeValue))
  )
```

```{r}
flood_model_clean <- flood_model_data %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(log_damage),
    !is.na(rain_1day_prior),
    !is.na(rain_3day_prior),
    !is.na(rain_7day_prior),
    !is.na(Population),
    !is.na(HousingUnits),
    !is.na(MedianHomeValue)
  )

nrow(flood_model_clean)

summary(flood_model_clean)
```
<!--
I ran a random forest model using:

all flood events (including ones with $0 damage)
rainfall variables
county variables
Result:
R² was basically 0
What that means:

The model couldn’t explain anything.

Why:

There were a lot of floods with zero damage, which made it hard for the model to learn anything meaningful.
-->

```{r}
set.seed(123)

train_index <- sample(
  seq_len(nrow(flood_model_clean)),
  size = 0.7 * nrow(flood_model_clean)
)

train_data <- flood_model_clean[train_index, ]
test_data  <- flood_model_clean[-train_index, ]

nrow(train_data)
nrow(test_data)
```

```{r}
rf_model <- randomForest(
  log_damage ~ rain_1day_prior + rain_3day_prior + rain_7day_prior +
    Population + HousingUnits + MedianHomeValue,
  data = train_data,
  ntree = 500,
  importance = TRUE
)

rf_model
```
```{r}
pred <- predict(rf_model, newdata = test_data)

rmse <- sqrt(mean((pred - test_data$log_damage)^2))
r2 <- cor(pred, test_data$log_damage)^2

rmse
r2

importance(rf_model)
varImpPlot(rf_model)
```
<!--
Step 5 focused on improving the first model. The original random forest included all flood and flash flood events, even those with zero property damage. That model performed very poorly, which suggested that the large number of zero-damage events was making it difficult for the model to detect meaningful patterns. To address this, I created a second version of the dataset that only kept events with property damage greater than zero. I then ran a new random forest model using the same predictors: 1-day prior rainfall, 3-day prior rainfall, 7-day prior rainfall, population, housing units, and median home value. This second model performed much better than the baseline model. The improvement suggested that removing zero-damage events helped reduce noise and made the relationship between rainfall, county characteristics, and damage easier to detect.
-->

```{r}
flood_model2 <- flood_model_clean %>%
  filter(DAMAGE_PROPERTY_NUM > 0)
```

```{r}
set.seed(123)

train_index2 <- sample(
  seq_len(nrow(flood_model2)),
  size = 0.7 * nrow(flood_model2)
)

train_data2 <- flood_model2[train_index2, ]
test_data2  <- flood_model2[-train_index2, ]

rf_model2 <- randomForest(
  log_damage ~ rain_1day_prior + rain_3day_prior + rain_7day_prior +
    Population + HousingUnits + MedianHomeValue,
  data = train_data2,
  ntree = 500,
  importance = TRUE
)
```

```{r}
pred2 <- predict(rf_model2, newdata = test_data2)

rmse2 <- sqrt(mean((pred2 - test_data2$log_damage)^2))
r22 <- cor(pred2, test_data2$log_damage)^2

rmse2
r22
```

<!--
Step 5 focused on improving the first model. The original random forest included all flood and flash flood events, even those with zero property damage. That model performed very poorly, which suggested that the large number of zero-damage events was making it difficult for the model to detect meaningful patterns. To address this, I created a second version of the dataset that only kept events with property damage greater than zero. I then ran a new random forest model using the same predictors: 1-day prior rainfall, 3-day prior rainfall, 7-day prior rainfall, population, housing units, and median home value. This second model performed much better than the baseline model. The improvement suggested that removing zero-damage events helped reduce noise and made the relationship between rainfall, county characteristics, and damage easier to detect.-->

```{r}
flood_model3 <- flood_model2 %>%
  mutate(
    rain_pop = rain_3day_prior * Population,
    rain_housing = rain_3day_prior * HousingUnits
  )
```

```{r}
set.seed(123)

train_index3 <- sample(
  seq_len(nrow(flood_model3)),
  size = 0.7 * nrow(flood_model3)
)

train_data3 <- flood_model3[train_index3, ]
test_data3  <- flood_model3[-train_index3, ]

rf_model3 <- randomForest(
  log_damage ~ rain_1day_prior + rain_3day_prior + rain_7day_prior +
    Population + HousingUnits + MedianHomeValue +
    rain_pop + rain_housing,
  data = train_data3,
  ntree = 500,
  importance = TRUE
)

pred3 <- predict(rf_model3, newdata = test_data3)

rmse3 <- sqrt(mean((pred3 - test_data3$log_damage)^2))
r23 <- cor(pred3, test_data3$log_damage)^2

rmse3
r23
```

```{r}
importance(rf_model2)
varImpPlot(rf_model2)
```
<!--
Step 7 focused on simplifying the model based on the variable importance results. The importance output showed that the 3-day and 7-day rainfall variables were not contributing much and in some cases appeared to hurt performance. In contrast, 1-day prior rainfall remained useful, while population, housing units, and median home value were consistently stronger predictors. Based on that, I created a fourth and final model using only 1-day prior rainfall, population, housing units, and median home value. This model performed slightly better than the second model and was the best overall version. The final results suggest that flood-related property damage in this dataset is explained more by county exposure variables, such as population and housing, than by rainfall totals alone. They also suggest that short-term rainfall is more useful for prediction than longer rainfall accumulation windows.

Overall, the modeling process showed that the most useful improvements came from filtering out zero-damage events and simplifying the predictor set. More complex versions of the model did not perform better. The final model was still limited in predictive power, which is reasonable given that flood damage is influenced by many factors that were not included in the dataset, such as drainage conditions, elevation, infrastructure, and differences in local reporting. Even so, the analysis still provided useful insight into which variables were most related to damage and helped identify a more defensible final model.
-->

```{r}
rf_model4 <- randomForest(
  log_damage ~ rain_1day_prior +
    Population + HousingUnits + MedianHomeValue,
  data = train_data2,
  ntree = 500,
  importance = TRUE
)

pred4 <- predict(rf_model4, newdata = test_data2)

rmse4 <- sqrt(mean((pred4 - test_data2$log_damage)^2))
r24 <- cor(pred4, test_data2$log_damage)^2

rmse4
r24
```
